lubidine divitias suas vincere nequeunt. at nobis est domi inopia, foris
aes alienum, mala res, spes multo asperior; denique quid reliqui

imperare parati estis.’

passage: hic ego ipsam rem definiam, mulierem nullam nominabo; tantum in medio

passage: audistis cum pro se diceret, audistis antea cum accusaret (defendendi haec

forte fallebat, ratio et bonis artibus instituta et cura et vigiliis elaborata. atqui

etiam non numquam impeditus hoc, quicquid est, quod nos facimus in dicendo,
quoquo modo facimus non modo agendo, verum etiam cogitando possit
sustinere.

exemplars.question: 2022-2d
exemplars.source: OCR, Exemplar candidate work, H443/03 Prose Literature (Tacitus), June 2022

segments.t: Tacitus creates a lively description of Otho by detailing the responses elicited by the possibility of his succession.
He writes,
‘et rumoribus nihil silentio transmittentium, quia Vinio vidua filia, caelebs Otho, gener ac socer destinabantur,’
which translates to,

‘and in the gossip of the people, who let nothing pass by in silence, Otho was being marked out as the son-in-law and Vinius the father-in-law, because Otho was a bachelor and Vinius had an unmarried daughter.’
Here,
the consonance of ‘m’ and ‘n’
mimics the impression of the people’s gossip, thus reflecting the animated response created by Otho.
Also, Tacitus asserts,
‘credo et rei publicae curam subisse, frustra a Nerone translatae si apud Othonem relinqueretur,’
meaning,
‘I believe that concern for the state influenced Galba, as it would have been removed from Nero in vain if it were to be left in the hands of Otho.’
The alliteration of ‘c’
places further emphasis on Tacitus’ remark, and the argument that Otho can be likened to Nero gives the impression that he is a man of excess.
Tacitus also creates a lively portrait of Otho by revealing his immorality.
He writes,
‘namque Otho pueritiam incuriose, adulescentiam petulanter egerat, gratus Neroni aemulatione luxus,’
which means,
‘for Otho had spent his boyhood negligently, his youth under no restraints, being pleasing to Nero as an imitation of his lust,’
and here
the balanced phrasing of ‘pueritiam incuriose, adulescentiam’ (with the nouns followed by adverbs)
creates the impression that Otho’s recklessness has endured throughout his life, without ever changing.
In addition, Tacitus foregrounds Otho’s corruption in,
‘eoque Poppaeam Sabinam, principale scortum, ut apud conscium libidinum deposuerat, donec Octaviam uxorem amolietur,’
which translates to,
‘and for that Nero left with him, as into the keeping of one who was aware of his lusts, Poppaea Sabina, the imperial whore, until he could get rid of his wife Octavia.’
The use of such objectifying language in describing this action, such as ‘principale scortum’ and ‘amolietur’,
creates a lively portrait of Otho by revealing him as a man who condones and is complicit in the misogynistic treatment of women.
Additionally, Tacitus’ description of Otho is made more lively by his revelation of Otho’s positive attributes and the support he garnered.
He writes,
‘Otho comiter administrata provincia primus in partes transgressus nec segnis et, donec bellum fuit, inter praesentes splendidissimus,’
which means,

‘after he had administered the province graciously, Otho was the first to join Galba’s party, and he was not inactive, and, for as long as the war last, he was the most brilliant among his immediate supporters.’
Tacitus’ use of such positive language in reference to Otho, with the superlative of ‘splendidissimus’,
depicts Otho as a hard-working and exceptional man.
Furthermore, this is also shown when Tacitus writes,
‘spem adoptionis statim conceptam acrius in dies rapiebat,’
meaning,
‘he conceived at once the hope for the adoption, and was grasping for it more eagerly each day.’
Here,
the language of immediacy and fervour which Tacitus utilises, such as, ‘statim,’ ‘acrius,’ and ‘rapiebat’,
highlights Otho’s activity and passion in striving for his ambition of the adoption.
Otho’s portrait is also made lively by Tacitus’ reference to his supporters,
in,
‘faventibus plerisque militum, prona in eum aula Neronis ut similem,’
which translates to,
‘with the majority of the soldiers favouring him, and Nero’s court inclined to him as being like Nero.’
The liveliness here is conveyed in the hyperbaton of ‘prona’ and ‘aula’,
as this enables these words to surround ‘eum’ in order to imitate the support which enveloped Otho.
Thus, Tacitus creates a lively portrait of Otho by detailing this simultaneously corrupt yet extraordinary man, and the reactions to him.

exemplars.commentary: This is a very good response (Level 5). The point about how Otho spent his boyhood and youth negligently is excellent: a good quote with accurate translation. Then a literary device is identified (balanced phrasing), and the effect of this balance is well developed. There is a wide range of points which covers the entirety of the passage. The question is directly answered by an appropriate selection of evidence.

exemplars.question: 2022-2d
exemplars.source: OCR, Exemplar candidate work, H443/03 Prose Literature (Tacitus), June 2022

segments.t: Tacitus creates a lively portrait of Otho by linking him to Titus Vinius, a man who Tacitus has made clear that people hated him.
“Othonis ac Titi Vinii amicitia”
(the friendship of Otho and Titus Vinius)
is also shown to be well known as
“gener ac socer destinabanter”
(they were called son-in-law and father-in-law)
even though
“caelebs Otho”
(Otho was single)
This variatio
mirrors the many different ways Otho and Titus are linked together
and the fact Otho is so close to a hated man makes him more interesting.
Otho’s history with Nero also makes him interesting.
Tacitus remarks on how Otho
“pueritiam incuriose, adulescentiam petulanter egerat”
(spent his boyhood carelessly, adolescense recklessly)
and
the asyndeton
helps to show just how quickly it went by.
Otho is also said to
“Neroni aemulatione luxus”
(copy the luxury of Nero)
which seemed to include
“Poppaean Sabinam, principale scortum”
(Poppaea Sabina, the imperial whore)
The juxtaposition of “principale scortum”
is really meant to demean Poppaea by combining such a high class title with a vulgar word and that fact that it is neuter objectifys her into something to be passed around.
But the fact Otho is trusted with her shows Nero’s fondness of him until he is
“suspectum in eadem Poppaea”
(suspected in the case of the same Poppea)
. Otho is
“specie legationis seposuit”
(exiled under the cover of a legate)
which shows that Nero still cared about Otho’s reputation.
Otho’s time during and after Lusitania adds to the lively portrait of Otho.
Otho
“comiter administrata provincia”
(governs the province in a friendly way)
and
“nec segnis et, donec bellum fuit”
(is not lazy, as long as there is war)
The brevitas of the second part of the statement
seems to undermine the compliment given in the first half.
Otho also seems obsessed with being adopted by Galba as he wanted it
“statim conceptam”
(as soon as it was concieved)
and
“acrius in dies rapiebat”
(was wanting it more sharply everyday)
. Otho is
“faventibus plerisque militum”
(favoured by very many soldiers)
which is very useful to Otho later
and is seen as
“similem”
(similar)
to Nero by his palace and as it was placed at
a point of emphasis
, the similarities between Nero and Otho must be important.

exemplars.commentary: There is good engagement here (Level 4) showing some points which however are not always developed. The point about gener ac socer is good, but the literary device of variation is not sufficiently pointed out or explained. The range of points is also a little limited – more material is needed if such responses are to reach the higher levels. The point about Otho being similem is relevant (as is the note about the emphatic placement of the adjective), but there is limitation in the amount of Latin and context/quotation offered.

exemplars.question: 2022-2d
exemplars.source: OCR, Exemplar candidate work, H443/03 Prose Literature (Tacitus), June 2022

segments.t: Tacitus creates a lively portrait of Otho by describing his
‘pueritiam incuriose’
(indifferent childhood)
the emotive use of the word ‘incuriose’ (indifferent)
shows in which ways he was similar to Nero and very different from Galba.
He spent some of his youth with Nero emulting in excess with his lusts. As we know what Nero was like this helps us better understand what Otho will be like.
This is further the case when it is stated
‘prona in eum pala Neronis ut similem’
(The palace was bias to him as he was similar to Nero)
The emphatic posistion of ‘similem’ (similar)
further highlights just how similar they both were.
Tacitus creates a lively portrait of Otho by highlighting the vices of him.
He lusted for Poppaea Sabina the
‘principale scortum’
(cheif whore)
which is what lead to him being exiled to Lustiania by Nero.
However, to contrast this Tacitus then portrays the good things in which Otho had done. For example, upon being exiled he was not inactive an
‘bellum fuit, inter praesentes splendidissimus’
(when in war, he was in as one of the most distinguished)
Tacitus creates a lively portrait by talking about Otho’s companions.
Not only does he talk about Nero and Poppaea as the people he chooses to surround himself with but he also talks about the close relationship he has with Titus Vinius even describing them as
‘quia Vinio vidua filia, caelebs Otho’
(father-in-law and son in law and Vinius had an unmarried daughter and Otho was a bachelor)
. This is the rumour that was spread by the people.
This creates a lively portrait as we see how others perceive him.
Furthermore, by stating who he associates with we can perhaps judge his character.

exemplars.commentary: There is some engagement in this response (Level 3). Noticeably, the response is on the short side and this lack of range of points will inevitably lead to a lower level. The response begins with some erroneous translation regarding the ‘indifferent childhood’. The point about the court of Nero being similar to Otho is a good quote/translation, but the emphatic position is not properly explained and developed. The point about the principale scortum also shows just some engagement (without a fuller quote or context however which again leads towards a lower level).

exemplars.question: 2022-4a
exemplars.source: OCR, Exemplar candidate work, H443/03 Prose Literature (Tacitus), June 2022

segments.t: Firstly, Tacitus makes this passage a striking piece of writing due to the army boasting about the killing of a man, which is extremely shocking, due to the profound permanence and sadness of death:
“certatim ostentantibus cruentas manus”
(with men showing their bloodied hands in competition).

This statement shocks the reader, since it is particularly striking how soldiers feel the need to show off that they have killed others, and even turning it into almost a game, comparing who has killed the most;
this is highlighted by the emphatic promotion of “certatim”.
The promotion of “cruentas” to before its noun, “manus”,
also portrays the extent of the violence,
while the sarcastic use of “pulchrum” in the next clause to describe the killing
shows Tacitus’ disapproval.
Vitellius, the next emperor, also found
“more than 120 letters of those demanding a reward on account of some notable deed on that day”
(plures quam centum viginti libellos praemium exposcentium ob aliquam notabilem illa die operam).

The multitude of 120 shows just how many men have committed the most serious crime possible, while the demand for a “praemium” shows how the soldiers are even proud of their murdering, which is shockingly disgraceful.
Tacitus also makes this passage striking by the gory account of Galba’s dead corpse:
“diu neglectum et licentia tenebrarum plurimis ludibriis vexatum”
(neglected for a long time and abused with very many insults under the freedom of darkness).
The hyperbole of “diu”
conveys just how little care was taken over saving Galba’s corpse and keeping it intact,
while the violent nature of “vexatum” and superlative “plurimis”
highlights just how many gory wounds his body sustained – even after he had died, meaning people added unneeded attacks to his long-dead body.
Further abuse of his body is conveyed via
“cremato iam corpori admixtum est”
([his head] was added to his body – already burnt),
in which the promotion of “cremato” to before “corpori”
emphasises how his body has been set on fire, which is a striking and gory detail.
Even Galba’s head was abused, which is shown in the following:
“caput per lixas calonesque suffixum laceratumque”
(his head was fixed to a pole and mangled by camp-followers and attendants).
This quotation shows the extent of abuse Galba’s head sustained,
which is conveyed by the juxtaposition of the gory “suffixum” and “laceratum”
(the former again showing the boasting of the soldiers),
while the pleonasm of “lixas” and “calones”
shows just how many people abused Galba’s head in such a violent, shocking way.
Finally, this passage is made striking by Tacitus through his presentation of Galba’s fall from imperial power.
Despite being a former emperor, Vitellius (emperor after Otho) sought to avenge Galba and kill his assassins
“non honori Galbae”
(not for the honour of Galba).

This is particularly striking, due to the lack of respect shown by Vitellius to his predecessor, even if he was not the most successful emperor: we as a reader would still expect a certain amount of respect, which is clearly not the case,
due to the tersity and matter-of-fact nature of such an authorial comment.
Furthermore, the contrast between Galba being the most powerful figure in Rome, yet only being buried
“in a modest tomb in his private gardens”
(humili sepultura in privatis eius hortis),
is striking: this is such a rapid fall from power and honour.
The personification of the tomb being modest, as well as the promotion of “humili” and “privatis” to before their nouns,
conveys just how little public respect was shown at Galba’s burial, which is striking for an emperor who was even supported by the general population until recently.

exemplars.commentary: This is a very good response (Level 5). The candidate engages very well with how striking the passage is: directly answering the question is a hallmark of a top-level response. The point about the soldiers vying to show off their bloody hands has a good Latin quote, well translated, with excellent discussion not just about a literary device (promotion of certatim), but also in terms of how the candidate develops the point as it is striking that the soldiers almost turn their actions into a game.

exemplars.question: 2022-4a
exemplars.source: OCR, Exemplar candidate work, H443/03 Prose Literature (Tacitus), June 2022

segments.t: In this passage, Tacitus tells of the events surrounding the murder of Galba. This passage is significant, as Galba is a key character in this book.
This is a striking piece of writing as visceral imagery is used to describe Galba’s burial, as well as many people claiming responsibility for his murder.
Firstly, Galba’s burial is described through the sentence
“Galbae corpus diu neglectum et licentia tenebrarum plurimis ludibriis vexatum dispensator Argius e prioribus servis humili sepultura in privatis eius hortis contexit”

(The body of Galba, for a long time neglected and, in the freedom of the darkness, abused by very many indignities, did the steward Argius, one of his former slaves, cover him with a humble burial in his private gardens).
The lexical cluster of words of abuse such as “neglectum”, “licentia”, “tenebrarum”

is striking as Galba was the emperor of the state and despite his authority and status, he is treated in this way. What makes it more striking is that he is treated this way after death, and no one is showing Galba the respect that one often deserves after an untimely death.
His burial has a slight personal touch, as his ex-slave Argius covers his body, as no one else would do it.
Galba’s entire burial is bizarre, as it takes place in
“privatis eius hortis”
(his private gardens),

dissimilar to the funeral of another emperor. The reservedness and secrecy of Galba’s burial is striking as someone of his status is normally deserving of a larger, more respectful celebration of life.
It is clear through the smaller burial of Galba, people’s negative opinions of him.
Furthermore, this passage is striking through the way Galba’s body has been treated and the amount of people who are joyful in his death.
This is seen in the sentence
“caput per lixas calonesque suffixum laceratumque ante Patrobii tumulum postera demum die repertum et cremato iam corpori admixtum est”

(His head, strung up and lacerated by the camp-followers and the soldiers’ servants, before the temple of Patrobius, was at last on the following day found and was mixed in with his already cremated body).
Yet again, the visceral lexical choice of
“per lixas calonesque suffixum laceratumque”
creates dark and violent imagery in the readers’ heads, making this passage striking through its gore and disgust.
There is a lack of care for Galba as his head was
“postera demum die repertum”
(at last on the following day was found).
The unfinished participle “repertum”

displays how ‘unfinished’ Galba’s body was as his head was literally not attached to his body. This makes the passage striking and suspenseful as Galba does not receive the care and respect that an emperor should receive.
Finally, many people take pride and joy in Galba’s murder, as seen in the sentence

“praefixa contis capita gestabantur inter signa cohortium iuxta aquilam legionis, certatim ostentantibus cruentas manus qui occiderant, qui interfuerant, qui vere qui falso ut pulchrum et memorabile facinus iactabant”

(His head, attached to a pole, was carried about between the standards of the cohorts, equally between the eagle of the legion, while, in rivalry, they were showing their bloodstained hands, those who took part in the murder, who were there, who, genuinely or falsely, were bragging of their crime as something beautiful and memorable).
The multiple asyndetic balanced phrasing with the anaphora of “qui” in the phrase “qui occiderant ... facinus iactabant”

highlights the amount of people claiming to be there where Galba was killed, if they weren’t taking responsibility of the murder, making this passage striking as it is clear as how many people despised Galba and wanted him dead.

In conclusion, Tacitus makes this passage striking, mainly through the violent and visceral imagery used to describe Galba’s treatment after death and his burial. It is also striking as Tacitus reveals how many people are glad to see Galba dead.

exemplars.commentary: This is a good response (Level 4). The final point gives a long quotation which is well translated, and the candidate finds a literary device to discuss. Giving such a long translation without sufficient analysis limits this response to some extent: there is much that could be analysed in this portion to gain extra credit. A greater number of such analysed points could lead this response into Level 5.

exemplars.question: 2022-4a
exemplars.source: OCR, Exemplar candidate work, H443/03 Prose Literature (Tacitus), June 2022

segments.t: Tacitus makes this a striking piece of writing by describing horror of what has happened on that day.
“capita gestabantur inter signa cohortium”
(heads were raised between the standards of the cohorts)
which already creates a horrific image but to have them
“iuxta aquilam legionis”
(next to the legionary eagle)
creates a contrasts as the sign of the loyal soldiers, fighting for the good of Rome, is next to proof of brutal acts of violence.
The soldiers show off their
“cruentas manus”
(bloody hands)
which is more proof of the carnage that has taken place.
Tacitus also uses the repition of
“qui”
(those who)
to show the variety of things that happened which adds to the confusion of the day.
Tacitus shows the direct consequenses of these events.
The fact that
“plures quam centum viginti libellos”
(more than a hundred and twenty people)
expected a
“praemium”
(prize)
for their conduct on that day is chilling.
But Vitellius’ response of
“omnesque conquiri et interfici iussit”
(ordered them all to be found and killed)
is done for his own self-preservation,
“non honori Galbae”
(not to honour Galba).
The poor treatment of Galba’s body is also striking.
The body is
“licentia tenebrarum plurimis ludibriis vexatum”
(subjected to many liberties under the cover of darkness)
with the alliteration of ‘l’ linking the cover and the liberties.
Galba is buried in a
“humili”
(humble ceremony)
“in privatis eius hortis”
(in his private gardens)
by
“dispensator Argius e prioribus servis”
(the steward Argius out of his former servants)
which is not an appropriate burial for an emperor.
Galba’s head is also missing when he is buried and, in a twist of irony, is found by the tomb of Patrobius, who was punished under Galba.
The fact the head was
“cremato iam corpori admixtum est”
(mixed in with his now cremated body)
creates a pitiful image of Galba.

exemplars.commentary: There are some good points here (leading to Level 3), but the lack of range and the lack of development inhibit this response. It begins well with a good Latin quote about the decapitated heads on display. Explaining how this is shocking as the heads are next to the eagle is also a good development. The lack of development begins when the candidate then selects just cruentas manus for comment. There is probably enough background context to justify credit here, but it is always risky as often examiners cannot find the necessary context. This is definitely the case when the word qui is selected for comment. This is a fragmented and isolated word which is not contextualised, and so any literary point (repetition) is invalidated without the accompanying context.

exemplars.question: csa-aeneid7
exemplars.source: OCR, A Level Latin Candidate Style Answers, H443/03 and H443/04 (2018)

segments.t: The first thing we are told about Circe’s land is that it is
‘untrodden’
– which means that no-one ever goes there.
The Trojans merely skirt the edge of it (
raduntur
), as Neptune sends the Trojans a favourable wind to prevent them from even trying to land there.
The shores are described as
dira
(‘dangerous’)
and full of boiling shallows
vada fervida
There is a weird never-ending sound of music and a strange smell of cedar wood.
Circe herself seems like a hermit, living alone and just doing her weaving and chanting all the time, probably spells.

The most menacing thing, however, is that there are lots of fierce animals – bears, boars, lions and wolves – that she keeps chained up around the place, and they are constantly howling and struggling to break out of their pens.
In line 8 the alliteration of the letter S
makes you think you can hear them
and
ululare
(line 9) reminds you of the sound made by wolves.
To make things worse, these aren’t even real animals, but just the
‘shapes’
of animals (
formae
) that Circe has turned
‘from the appearance of men’
hominum ex facie
) into monsters with her magic herbs, so it is lucky that the Trojans don’t go there or they too might be turned into animals.
Circe herself isn’t actually described by Virgil, but she obviously isn’t just an ordinary woman, as she is the daughter of the Sun, which gives her these frightening powers.

exemplars.commentary: This answer takes a thematic approach to the question, starting with a description of the land, then Circe and finally her victims. The discussion does sometimes come across as narrative, although the candidate has selected some sensible Latin. The candidate’s speculation on Circe could earn credit if it provided more substantial evidence from the text. Greater reference to the text would also be beneficial for the section on wild animals. Some points are missed. The first half in particular lacks stylistic discussion and the sibilance point needs development.

exemplars.question: csa-annals14
exemplars.source: OCR, A Level Latin Candidate Style Answers, H443/03 and H443/04 (2018)

segments.t: It is clear from the start of this passage that Nero is petrified by the thought of what Agrippina might do, now that she has worked out that it was no accident when she was nearly killed on Nero’s boat.
He is
‘out of his mind with fear’
pavore exanimis
) and thinks she will be arriving to get revenge any minute.
The repetition in
iam iamque
emphasises his panic.
He worries that she might attempt all sorts of awful things – start a slave rebellion, take over the army, or reveal all to the Senate and people.
Tacitus makes him pose to himself a rhetorical question:
quod contra subsidium sibi?
(what could help him now)
, which emphasises that he has no idea what to do to stop her.
Then he suddenly thinks of Burrus and Seneca, the people he usually depends on to get him out of a crisis.
The incomplete sentence
nisi quid Burrus et Seneca
underlines Nero’s panic, as if his mind is racing from one idea to another.
Burrus and Seneca, however, turn out to be useless. They just stand like dummies, each hoping that the other one will come up with something.
They are frightened that Nero will not be prepared to accept their usual cautious advice (
ne inriti dissuaderent
), and the comment
incertum an et ante ignaros
even suggests that they knew all about Nero’s problems already but hadn’t dared to get involved.

They probably know that, unless Agrippina can be stopped in time, this is the end of Nero’s reign, and yet they can’t think how to eliminate her. Even if Burrus ordered his troops to kill her, they would refuse to obey because of their loyalty to the memory of her grandfather Germanicus.
Finally, they sarcastically challenge Anicetus to finish what he promised but has failed to deliver (
perpetraret Anicetus promissa
) – a suitably brief and angry remark, emphasised by the alliteration of P and R and the position of perpetraret.
Anicetus really shows all the other three up.
Without any hesitation, in sharp contrast to the dithering of Seneca and Burrus, he coolly volunteers to organise Agrippina’s murder (
poscit summam sceleris
– another snappy phrase with striking word-order and alliteration).
At a stroke, Nero’s worries look like being solved – and by a mere freedman!
His relief is indicated by the hyperbolic statement
illo die dari imperium
, and the delayed position of the word
libertum
underlines his shock at who has turned out to be the saviour of his position.

exemplars.commentary: A very full and well-crafted analysis of the thrust and tone of the passage, backed up by plenty of apt citations of the Latin and attention to stylistic features.

exemplars.question: csa-sallust
exemplars.source: OCR, A Level Latin Candidate Style Answers, H443/03 and H443/04 (2018)

segments.t: In this speech Sallust presents Catiline as extremely persuasive and inspiring.
He begins by listing all the things that only the rich have – such as precious jewellery or big houses, paid for by extorting money from the poor –
to rouse envy and hostility in his audience.
He then constructs a similar list of the sufferings endured by the poor, such as poverty and debt, which make their lives hopeless (
spes multo asperior
) and leave them with nothing except a miserable soul (
miseram animam
In lines 10-11, the emphatic phrase
en illa illa ... libertas
is an extremely clever rhetorical flourish.
The separation of liberty from illa illa
suggests that the idea of liberty is now just out of reach but that it can be grasped if he is helped with overthrowing the republic.
As well as liberty, other ideas are suggested here to provide a sense of what might be, which would be very stirring to his supporters.
divitiae decus gloria
are presented as good reasons for joining Catiline.

Though not expressed through the word-order, as with libertas, the idea that glory and riches sit in front of them waiting to be grasped is a feature which would also be incredibly stirring to his audience.
Then Catiline gives a list of other positives to emerge from the conspiracy – for example,
bella spolia magnifice
(‘magnificent spoils of war’)
– which might have convinced others that it was worth their while to join him.
He also promises several things to reassure them of his loyalty both to the cause and to them.
The repetition of
vel imperatore vel milite
makes a nice contrast between a commander and a soldier.
Catiline makes it clear that he is willing to be either, depending on what is needed - though the fact that imperatore comes first suggests that he is more keen to be a commander.
This is a subtle persuasive technique, designed to subliminally show that he’s in charge, whilst saying that he can be used for whatever is necessary.
Next he promises that
‘neither my mind nor my body can take me away from you’
neque animus neque corpus a vobis aberit
The repetition of neque
illustrates how Catiline is there for his conspirators and the protection he is offering them.

However, by bringing Catiline’s mind and body into the speech, suggesting how it will never leave his followers, creates humour and mockery, as he is presented as being extremely desperate towards his followers.
This highlights Catiline’s pervasive nature, as he is offering security and protection as well as being enthusiastic about the conspiracy.

exemplars.commentary: A respectable attempt to maintain focus on the question and includes a limited number of stylistic features. Understanding of the passage is not totally convincing, however, and several ideas seem rather flimsy/ trivial.

exemplars.question: csa-verres
exemplars.source: OCR, A Level Latin Candidate Style Answers, H443/03 and H443/04 (2018)

segments.t: Cicero highlights the military achievements of famous Roman generals to show up Verres.
He uses many superlatives
to emphasise their conquests
- for example,
urbem ornatissimam
(‘a very decorated city’)
and
regem potentissimum
(‘a very powerful king’).
This makes Verres seem inadequate by comparison.
He says that L. Paulus overcame King Perses
vi ac virtute
(‘by force and courage’)
and that L. Mummius seized Corinth,
‘a very beautiful and most ornate city, very full of all things’.
Cicero also uses hyperbole in the words
imperium populi Romani dicionem
(‘the empire and dominion of the people of Rome’)
: this means the same but emphasises his achievements.
He uses a series of quick questions which get to the point.
The fact that he gives such a long list of the great feats of these men
draws attention to how much he admires them.
Then he says how he admires these great men even more because they didn’t keep their plunder but donated it to the Republic to display in public places in Rome and other cities.
This is emphasised by the increasing length of the phrases in
urbem totam templaque deorum omnesque Italiae partes
and Cicero’s constant use of words like
totam
and
omnes
He says
‘their homes were full of honour but free of statues and paintings’
– unlike Verres, who was only of lowly quaestorian rank, but plundered and kept for himself whatever he liked.
So Verres’ home is the opposite to theirs – full of statues and paintings, yet empty of virtue and honour!
When those honourable men conquered new places, they did it for Rome, not to gain material goods to showcase in their own homes.
Cicero finishes by apologising for going on so much about
‘the good old days’
antiqua et iam obsoleta

), but says that’s the sort of behaviour everyone expected in those days from people like generals and governors, so the prestige of the statues and other trophies reflected, not just on the individuals concerned, but on the whole community (
non solum hominum, verum etiam temporum illorum videantur
This is obviously intended to be another dig at Verres,
and perhaps also to inspire the jury in the trial to do something to help Rome to get back to the moral standards that everyone still admires about these famous figures of the past.

exemplars.commentary: A pretty comprehensive analysis of the content, incorporating a good range of stylistic features. Only slight vagueness here and there means that this response is not quite top-notch.

exemplars.question: 2024-1a

segments.t: Cicero then describes the reaction to his death:
“non solum propinquorum, sed etiam omnium Larinatium odio Oppianico, et illius adulescentis misericordia commoventur”
(not only the relatives but also all of the people of Larinum were strongly moved by hatred of Oppianicus and by pity for that young man).
The adversative particles “non solum” and “sed etiam” (not only, but also)
create an overwhelming sense of the number of people affected;
and the passive verb “commoventur” (strongly moved)
suggests they were overcome with emotion.
This creates a dramatic image of an outpouring of anger and grief.

exemplars.commentary: This candidate has produced an excellent point. A meaningful clause in Latin has been produced as evidence of the dramatic nature of the passage, and an accurate translation is given. The evidence is carefully directed to showing the drama in the passage. Relevant literary features are identified, and their effect is noted.

exemplars.question: 2024-2a

segments.t: Next we move on to a discussion of Sejanus’ choice of target: Drusus. We are told that he
‘ferebatur’
(was carried)
against Sejanus
‘recenti ira’
(by a recent rage).
This vividly captures the tensions within the imperial household and Sejanus and sets the scene for further drama.
Moreover, the chiastic arrangement of
‘impatiens aemuli’
(impatient of a rival)
and
‘animo commotior’
(more agitated in spirit)
emphasises Drusus’ rashness and hatred against Sejanus.
Stylistically,
‘verberaverat’
(struck)
is a strong word choice and not commonly used by Tacitus.
Together with the chiasmus and description of the quarrel above, this vividly portrays Drusus’ hostility, giving a good reason for Sejanus to begin with Drusus.

exemplars.commentary: The candidate has succeeded in tailoring a piece of evidence towards directly answering the question about how vivid the passage is. There is ample quotation of Latin which is embedded in the context of the overall narrative. The candidate has identified relevant stylistic features and given some development of their effect. The development (especially when explaining a chiasmus) could have been improved by explaining why the coming together of the two B words (or alternatively the separation of the A words) helps make the animosity of Drusus more vivid.

exemplars.question: 2025-3a

segments.t: Firstly, Cicero makes this a powerful attack on Clodia
with his sarcastic and deeply ironic claims in the first few lines not to be talking about a particular woman:
‘mulierem nullam nominabo’
(I shall not name any woman).
Yet, the exaggerated ‘m’ consonance in this line
could suggest his irony, and hint that he is referring exactly to Clodia.

With this irony, Cicero makes his attack on Clodia particularly biting since the audience no longer even need to hear her name - the jurors hear something to do with hedonism or a courtesan, and immediately link it to Clodia,
showing the depth of Cicero’s power to destroy her reputation.

exemplars.commentary: This is a good example of a well-developed point in a 15-mark response. The candidate has selected an appropriate piece of Latin which demonstrates Cicero’s method of attacking. The quotation is relevant and accurately translated. A piece of literary style is identified and discussed, before the whole point is clearly linked back to the question.

exemplars.question: 2025-4e

segments.t: … laetitiam testari’
(the neighbouring towns of Campania … testified their happiness).
Here, Tacitus emphasises this mocking response to Agrippina’s murder as Nero’s associates display happiness (‘laetitiam’) and even piety at the temples (‘templa’);
furthermore, the chiasmus of
‘adire templa … laetitiam testari’
(went to the temples … testified their happiness)
evokes a chilling sense of balance and harmony as Nero is flattered of her having murdered his mother.

exemplars.commentary: The candidate has judiciously selected a good piece of evidence which shows a vivid reaction to Agrippina’s death. The translation is accurate and the literary analysis, which is well developed, supports the point being made.

exemplars.question: 2026-2e

segments.t: … Agrippina would find a reason to remove him, without just cause.
But Narcissus’s opinion on Agrippina is made most clear by
‘ne quis ambigat decus pudorem corpus cuncta regno viliora habere?’
(lest anyone doubt that she held decency, shame, her body or anything cheaper than the kingdom?)
By giving us this list of matters of increasing scales of magnitude,
Tacitus emphasises that to Narcissus, Agrippina is defined as the worst kind of person, one whose ambition leads her to ignore all virtues.
Clearly, Narcissus’s thoughts on Agrippina are therefore demonstrated strongly.

exemplars.commentary: In this response, the candidate has quoted a relevant piece of Latin which is accurately translated. It is focused on the question as it reveals one of Narcissus’ thoughts. The candidate then notes the listing effect of all the things which Agrippina relegates in favour of seeking power which show how Narcissus thinks Agrippina is the worst kind of person.

exemplars.question: 2026-3d

segments.t: Firstly, Cicero uses anaphora
to emphasise the judges’ own experience of Caelius’ talent, forcibly making them remember the skill he showed.
He says:
‘audistis cum pro se diceret, audistis antea cum accusaret’
, meaning
‘you have heard him when he spoke on his defence, you have heard him beforehand when he was a prosecutor.’
The anaphora stresses the many examples there are of Caelius’ talent,
while the ongoing ‘a’ alliteration
emphasises the skill shown previously,
making for an impressive description of Caelius with the multitude of examples of times he showcased his oratory skill.

exemplars.commentary: This response demonstrates a strong point which typifies candidates’ responses in Level 5. There is a meaningful and well-selected Latin quote which is accurately translated and which shows exactly how impressive Caelius is. There is some development of the point in terms of how the anaphora (of audistis) calls attention to all the evidence of Caelius’ ability the judges have heard, and the evidence is linked to the question.

drills.context: Tacitus, Histories I.13 (June 2022, 2(d)*): In this passage, how does Tacitus create a lively portrait of Otho?
drills.latin: quia Vinio vidua filia, caelebs Otho, gener ac socer destinabantur
drills.weak: gener ac socer (son-in-law and father-in-law) is a good example of variatio.
drills.strong: Tacitus sets Vinio vidua filia beside caelebs Otho in mirrored order, then caps the pair with gener ac socer: the neat, gossipy balance reproduces the rumour-mill of Rome matching up a widowed daughter and a bachelor, so we meet Otho through the chatter he provokes, a lively and slightly scandalous introduction.
drills.source: OCR exemplar candidate work, H443/03 June 2022 (commentary on Exemplar 2); stronger version written for Classicalia
drills.why: OCR judged the point good but said the literary device was not sufficiently pointed out or explained.

drills.context: Tacitus, Histories I.13 (June 2022, 2(d)*): In this passage, how does Tacitus create a lively portrait of Otho?
drills.latin: faventibus plerisque militum, prona in eum aula Neronis ut similem
drills.weak: similem is in an emphatic position.
drills.strong: Tacitus holds similem back to the very last word of the passage: Nero’s court leans towards Otho ‘as one like him’, so the sentence ends by branding Otho a second Nero, a sharp final stroke that leaves the reader with a vivid and damning picture of the man.
drills.source: OCR exemplar candidate work, H443/03 June 2022 (commentaries on Exemplars 2 and 3); stronger version written for Classicalia
drills.why: The examiners noted that the emphatic position was relevant but not properly explained and developed.

drills.context: Virgil, Aeneid VII.10–24 (Candidate Style Answers, H443/04 1(a)*): How does Virgil make his description of Circe’s land menacing?
drills.latin: saetigerique sues atque in praesepibus ursi / saevire ac formae magnorum ululare luporum
drills.weak: In line 8 the alliteration of the letter S makes you think you can hear them.
drills.strong: The hissing s-sounds of saetigerique sues … praesepibus … saevire and the long, mournful vowels of ululare luporum let the reader hear the penned beasts raging and howling through the night; since these are men changed into animal shapes (formae), the very noise of the place carries the menace of Circe’s power.
drills.source: OCR, A Level Latin Candidate Style Answers (2018), commentary on the 8/15 answer; stronger version written for Classicalia
drills.why: The commentary says the sibilance point needs development: the stronger version says what the sound makes us hear and why that is menacing.

drills.context: Tacitus, Histories I.44 (June 2022, 4(a)*): How does Tacitus make lines 1–11 a striking piece of writing?
drills.latin: certatim ostentantibus cruentas manus qui occiderant, qui interfuerant, qui vere qui falso ut pulchrum et memorabile facinus iactabant
drills.weak: qui is repeated, which is effective.
drills.strong: The soldiers vie with one another (certatim) to show off their bloodstained hands, and the run of qui occiderant, qui interfuerant, qui vere qui falso sweeps in killers, onlookers and liars alike, all boasting of the murder as a glorious and memorable deed (pulchrum et memorabile facinus): the anaphora turns the killing of an emperor into a competition, which is what makes the scene so striking.
drills.source: OCR exemplar candidate work, H443/03 June 2022 (commentaries on Exemplars 1 and 3); stronger version written for Classicalia
drills.why: OCR said the word qui on its own is a fragmented, isolated word, so the point about repetition was invalidated without its context.

drills.context: Sallust, Bellum Catilinae 20 (Candidate Style Answers, H443/03 5(b)*): What makes Catiline’s words a stirring appeal to his supporters?
drills.latin: vel imperatore vel milite me utimini; neque animus neque corpus a vobis aberit
drills.weak: By bringing Catiline’s mind and body into the speech, suggesting how it will never leave his followers, creates humour and mockery, as he is presented as being extremely desperate towards his followers.
drills.strong: Catiline offers himself to them as either general or soldier (vel imperatore vel milite me utimini), then pledges neque animus neque corpus a vobis aberit: the balanced pairs and the repeated neque promise his whole self, mind and body, to the cause, so the appeal stirs his supporters with a leader’s total commitment to them.
drills.source: OCR, A Level Latin Candidate Style Answers (2018), commentary on the 11/15 answer; stronger version written for Classicalia
drills.why: The commentary found several ideas flimsy; this one also turns away from the question, which asks what makes the appeal stirring.

drills.context: Cicero, pro Caelio 57 (June 2026, 1(e)*): How does Cicero make this passage a strong defence of Caelius?
drills.latin: quibus omnia committantur, per quos gerantur, qui versentur isdem in voluptatibus
drills.weak: The polyptoton of qui is emphatic.
drills.strong: Cicero uses the polyptoton to direct the judges’ attention to the nature of Clodia’s house, as the polyptoton stresses the myriad ways in which the house is utterly abnormal.
drills.why: The stronger point says what the device does to the judges and ties it to the defence of Caelius.

drills.context: Cicero, pro Caelio 67 (June 2025, 1(d)*): How does Cicero ridicule the young men in this passage?
drills.latin: alia fori vis est, alia triclinii, alia subselliorum ratio, alia lectorum
drills.weak: Cicero uses the anaphora of alia.
drills.strong: The relentless repetition of alia helps to set up a series of binary opposites which reinforces in the minds of the jurors that Clodia’s ridiculous associates are totally at odds with the seriousness and skill required for speaking in a Roman court.
drills.why: Spotting the anaphora earns little on its own; the credit comes from showing how it ridicules the young men.

drills.context: Tacitus, Annals IV.3 (June 2024, 2(a)*): How does Tacitus make this a vivid account of the first steps in Sejanus’ plot?
drills.latin: intenderat Seiano manus et contra tendentis os verberaverat
drills.weak: There is a chiasmus here, which makes the sentence emphatic.
drills.strong: The chiasmus sets the two violent verbs, intenderat and verberaverat, at either end and brings Sejanus and the hands and face of the fight together in the middle, so the word order acts out the brawl: Drusus raises his fists at Sejanus and strikes him in the face as he squares up. The animosity of Drusus becomes vivid, and so does the insult that gives Sejanus his motive.
drills.source: OCR examiners’ report, H443/03 June 2024; stronger version written for Classicalia
drills.why: The examiners asked for an explanation of why the arrangement of the words makes Drusus’ animosity more vivid; naming the chiasmus is only the start.

drills.context: Cicero, pro Caelio 67 (June 2025, 1(d)*): How does Cicero ridicule the young men in this passage?
drills.latin: alveusne ille an equus Troianus fuerit, qui tot invictos viros muliebre bellum gerentes tulerit ac texerit
drills.weak: Cicero mentions the equus Troianus, the Trojan horse.
drills.strong: Cicero asks whether the bath-tub (alveusne ille) was a Trojan horse that carried and concealed so many unconquered heroes (tot invictos viros) waging a woman’s war (muliebre bellum gerentes): the mock-epic comparison inflates the ambush in the baths into the fall of Troy, and the clash between invictos viros and muliebre bellum makes Clodia’s young men absurd.
drills.source: OCR examiners’ report, H443/03 June 2025; stronger version written for Classicalia
drills.why: The report criticised answers that pick out words with easily recognisable English meanings, such as equus Troianus, without showing what they do in context.

drills.context: Cicero, Pro Cluentio 4 (June 2024, 1(a)*): How does Cicero make this a dramatic account of events?
drills.latin: se nomen Oppianici, si interfectum Marcum Aurium comperisset, delaturum esse testatur
drills.weak: Aulus Aurius swears that he will destroy Oppianicus, which is a dramatic threat.
drills.strong: In front of a crowd in the forum, and in a very loud voice, Aulus Aurius swears that he will bring a prosecution against Oppianicus (nomen … delaturum esse) if he finds that Marcus Aurius has been killed: the public threat builds anticipation, which is realised when the announcement of the killing follows.
drills.source: OCR examiners’ report, H443/03 June 2024; stronger version written for Classicalia
drills.why: Many candidates confused delaturum (denounce, prosecute) with deleturum (destroy); a misread verb changes the whole point.

drills.context: Tacitus, Annals IV.3 (June 2024, 2(a)*): How does Tacitus make this a vivid account of the first steps in Sejanus’ plot?
drills.latin: hanc ut amore incensus adulterio pellexit
drills.weak: Sejanus drove Livia to adultery, which shows how violent he is.
drills.strong: Sejanus, as if inflamed with love (ut amore incensus), enticed Livia into adultery (adulterio pellexit): ut casts doubt on the passion, and pellexit shows seduction as the first move of a calculated plot, which makes his scheming vivid.
drills.source: OCR examiners’ report, H443/03 June 2024; stronger version written for Classicalia
drills.why: The report notes that pellexit (‘he enticed’) was often mistranslated as ‘he drove’, which changes the picture of Sejanus.

drills.context: Cicero, Pro Cluentio 4 (June 2024, 1(a)*): How does Cicero make this a dramatic account of events?
drills.latin: interim brevi tempore illi, qui erant in agrum Gallicum profecti, Larinum revertuntur: interfectum esse Marcum Aurium renuntiant
drills.weak: Then the men who had gone to the Gallic territory came back to Larinum and reported that Marcus Aurius had been killed.
drills.strong: The news follows hard on Aurius’ threat (interim brevi tempore), told in two short historic presents, revertuntur … renuntiant, with interfectum esse placed first in the report: the threat is suddenly realised, and the blunt announcement strikes the reader as it struck Larinum.
drills.source: OCR examiners’ report, H443/03 June 2024; stronger version written for Classicalia
drills.why: The examiners rewarded answers that captured the drama, such as the anticipation after the threat, over those that simply narrated the events in order.

comments.text: Centres have become more aware of the need for developed analysis in 15-mark response questions: quoting a meaningful portion of Latin, then translating and discussing it in order to answer the question.
For 15-mark questions, candidates should be encouraged to quote and translate whole Latin phrases.
In some rare cases, the entire response was limited by having no reference at all to the Latin texts.
Fragmentary approaches which zone in on isolated words are unlikely to be credited.
focused too much on single isolated words, or words with English translations of Latin words which were easily recognisable (e.g. equus Troianus)
comments.source: OCR examiners’ report, H443/03 June 2025 (candidates who did less well)

comments.text: produced undeveloped analysis in 15-mark responses, often retelling the narrative with English paraphrases, or picking out isolated words with obvious English derivations but which did not show knowledge of their context in the passage
comments.source: OCR examiners’ report, H443/03 June 2024 (candidates who did less well)

comments.text: The most successful responses were able to capture the drama in this scene rather than simply narrating what happened in a linear progression through the passage.

While many scripts were extremely impressive, it was noticeable that a sizeable number were very narrative-heavy in their approaches. These responses tended to repeat the narrative of the text with some analysis of particular word choices but often neglecting the rich literary features that the texts contained.
In some cases, there was also a tendency to simply go through the narration of the passage to show how interesting it was. Greater levels of (stylistic) analysis would help prevent this shortcoming.
produced insightful responses to 15-mark questions by providing relevant evidence from the Latin texts and detailed discussion of relevant literary devices
comments.source: OCR examiners’ report, H443/03 June 2024 (candidates who did well)

comments.text: contained detailed discussion of relevant literary devices, both identifying these features and explaining their effects well
comments.source: OCR examiners’ report, H443/03 June 2025 (candidates who did well)

comments.text: Literary features can then be further analysed, and their relevance carefully explained.

In Question 1(d), most candidates were able to spot the obvious anaphora of alia which Cicero deployed, and assume that credit is gained merely by stating this fact. Better responses were able to suggest, for example, that the relentless repetition of alia helps to set up a series of binary opposites which reinforces in the minds of the jurors that Clodia’s ridiculous associates are totally at odds with the seriousness and skill required for speaking in a Roman court.
Knowledge of the style of authors was also in evidence, though at times the development of these points could be stronger in order to point out the effects of such devices.
At times, Cicero’s stylistic devices were merely alluded to without any development and such points were unlikely to be given marks.

Less successful responses tended simply to state that the polyptoton is emphatic. More successful responses took time to develop the point by stating that Cicero uses the polyptoton to direct the judges’ attention to the nature of Clodia’s house, as the polyptoton stresses the myriad ways in which the house is utterly abnormal.

The development (especially when explaining a chiasmus) could have been improved by explaining why the coming together of the two B words (or alternatively the separation of the A words) helps make the animosity of Drusus more vivid.
did not appreciate or evaluate the wealth of literary and rhetorical devices
comments.source: OCR examiners’ report, H443/03 June 2025 (candidates who did less well)

comments.text: Several candidates seemed to find the use of litotes at times when an author made a negation. It should be noted that litotes is a literary device in which an author uses an understatement (often through mentioning the negative of a positive quality) which has the effect of adding an ironic tone or downplaying some fact.

However, many obvious features of Tacitus’ typical repertoire (chiasmus, ellipsis, historic present tense) were not always commented on. Candidates should be encouraged to explore these aspects of Tacitus’ style and gain appropriate credit as a result.
Candidates were able to identify a range of emotions from outrage to sorrow and indignation, all of which were explained with well-selected evidence.
15-mark responses were focused on the question being asked, e.g. how the passage is ‘dramatic’, etc.
comments.source: OCR examiners’ report, H443/03 June 2024 (candidates who did well)

comments.text: Both content and use of language should be linked to the original question – e.g. how is a passage lively, or vivid, or how does it show an impressive character?
The key word ‘outrage’ triggered many focused responses as candidates enjoyed exploring the invective against Sassia which was geared towards provoking such outrage.
Candidates focused well on the trigger word ‘ridicule’ to bring out the humour and sarcasm of the passage which belittles Clodia and the men she sent.
A piece of literary style is identified and discussed, before the whole point is clearly linked back to the question.

A range of points should be taken from the whole passage: sometimes, candidates offer perhaps multiple points of analysis on the same Latin quote which restricts the attention they give to other parts of the passage.
A large number of candidates confused (nomen) delaturum (report, denounce) with deleturum, resulting in many statements that Aurius would destroy Oppianicus.
In a notable number of responses, pellexit (‘he enticed’) was mistranslated as ‘he drove’ Livia to adultery.

The phrase lautos iuvenes mulieris beatae ac nobilis familiares caused a few problems – firstly, some candidates confused the adjectival agreements to talk about ‘noble friends’, etc., while a significant few confused lautos (‘elegant, spruced up’) with laudatos (‘praised’).

There was confusion about understanding what exactly Tacitus meant by saying that the appearance of landscapes does not change like human expressions can, while some candidates took obversabatur as observabat, thinking Nero was just observing the landscape rather than the landscape imposing itself menacingly on Nero.

A few candidates got a little confused at times over the number of names in the passage (Narcissus, Claudius, Britannicus, Nero, Agrippina) but on the whole candidates who knew how to translate well and develop their points scored in the higher levels.
A few candidates seemed to mix up Agrippina and Poppaea in places, thinking that Tacitus was conveying Agrippina’s words when really Poppaea was speaking.

As often happens, a few candidates spent too much time on the 15-mark questions and ended up having to finish the 20-mark essay abruptly. The importance of good timing should be noted again by all centres.
It is always worth asking: are candidates spending too much time on the 15-mark questions?
There is ample quotation of Latin which is embedded in the context of the overall narrative.
